MetaPI: Constructing Prompt Injection Benchmarks from LLM Agent Benchmark

Peiran Wang, Chong Xiang, Wenjie Qu, Ying Li, Jiaheng Zhang, G. Edward Suh, Yuan Tian
University of California, Los Angeles; NVIDIA; University of California, Berkeley; National University of Singapore

MetaPI is a new toolkit that converts existing agent utility benchmarks into end-to-end indirect prompt-injection tests. An indirect prompt injection is a malicious instruction hidden in content that an agent reads while using tools. MetaPI reuses realistic tasks, environments, and infrastructure, then identifies injection points and generates attack objectives rather than relying on a small static attack set.

Why it matters: If you evaluate tool-using agents, this offers a way to test security across the same workflows used to measure task success, reducing the mismatch between utility and security evaluations

Flock Safety, whose drones were once reserved for police departments, is now offering them for private-sector security, the company announced today, with potential customers including businesses intent on curbing shoplifting. 

Companies in the US can now place Flock’s drone docking stations on their premises. If the company has a waiver from the Federal Aviation Administration to fly beyond visual line of sight (these are becoming easier to get), its security team can fly the drones within a certain radius, often a few miles. 

“Instead of a 911 call [that triggers the drone], it’s an alarm call,” says Keith Kauffman, a former police chief who now directs Flock’s drone program. “It’s still the same type of response.”

Kauffman walked through how the drone program might work in the case of retail theft: If the security team at a store like Home Depot, for example, saw shoplifters leave the store, then the drone, equipped with cameras, could be activated from its docking station on the roof.

“The drone follows the people. The people get in a car. You click a button,” he says, “and you track the vehicle with the drone, and the drone just follows the car.” 

The video feed of that drone might go to the company’s security team, but it could also be automatically transmitted directly to police departments.

The company says it’s in talks with large retailers but doesn’t yet have any signed contracts. The only private-sector company Kauffman named as a customer is Morning Star, a California tomato processor that uses drones to secure its distribution facilities. Flock will also pitch the drones to hospital campuses, warehouse sites, and oil and gas facilities. 

It’s worth noting that the FAA is currently drafting new rules for how it grants approval to pilots flying drones out of sight, and it’s not clear if Flock’s use case would be allowed under the currently proposed guidance.

The company’s expansion to the private sector follows the rise of programs launched by police departments around the country to deploy drones as first responders. In such programs, law enforcement sends drones to a scene to provide visuals faster than an officer can get there. 

Flock has arguably led this push, and police departments have claimed drone-enabled successes, like a supply drop to a boy lost in the Colorado wilderness. But the programs have also sparked privacy worries, concerns about overpolicing in minority neighborhoods, and lawsuits charging that police departments should not block public access to drone footage. 

Other technologies Flock offers, like license plate readers, have drawn recent criticism for the ease with which federal US immigration agencies, including ICE and CBP, could look at data collected by local police departments amid President Trump’s mass deportation efforts.

Flock’s expansion into private-sector security is “a logical step, but in the wrong direction,” says Rebecca Williams, senior strategist for the ACLU’s privacy and data governance unit. 

Williams cited a growing erosion of Fourth Amendment protections—which prevent unlawful search and seizure—in the online era, in which the government can purchase private data that it would otherwise need a warrant to acquire. Proposed legislation to curb that practice has stalled, and Flock’s expansion into the private sector would exacerbate the issue, Williams says.

“Flock is the Meta of surveillance technology now,” Williams says, referring to the amount of personal data that company has acquired and monetized. “This expansion is very scary.”

What are the visions of the post-AGI future in San Francisco? Many think we're all going to die, but even the "positive" visions seem rather dystopian. Here, I wrote about "handoverism," which involves handing control of the future to an AGI God, with humans outside the loop.
https://t.co/bLxgiG65vi

We are on the cusp of RSI or recursive self-improvement: this means that AI systems can self-improve, without the need for human intervention. This means our world stands to be transformed in what many call “the singularity”. I moved to SF around three weeks ago and one of the things I have been trying to understand is where we are heading, at least according to those developing the tech.

The worst scenarios are plainly bleak: all of us, or vast numbers of us, die. But what is striking to me is how little reassurance even some of the happiest scenarios offer. But one common and ostensibly optimistic vision is known as “handoverism”: humanity cedes control of its future to a godlike AI and we become the comfortably maintained inhabitants of a civilisation whose direction is no longer ours to decide. It is difficult to see what democracy would mean in such a world, or where the consent of most of humanity to the instantiation of such a regime enters the picture.

The permanent displacement of human labour is treated almost as a given. At the same time, there is scarcely any satisfying answer to the question of how we might remain useful to one another. Even our relationships seem uncertain. The promised utopia looks to me much closer to a kind of dystopia.

“It’s not my preferred outcome,” someone working at one of the big labs told me, “but once we achieve superintelligence, which we cannot stop at this point, I cannot see any other option for where humanity will go.” Then, after a pause, he added: “It is still much better than what I actually fear most, which is that we might all die.”

He sounded resigned, as if the question of what humans would be for (apparently not much?) had already been settled somewhere else and by someone else. All that remains, it seems, is to wait for this pre-destined fate to unfold before our eyes.

But I do not think that is the case. I believe we always have a choice and that we should try and steer this technology in a way that maintains our agency and control. And even if that looks hard and daunting, the immensity of the stakes here make it worth trying at least.

I do not know whether the handoverist vision will come to pass. That the people building this technology consider it plausible, and often desirable, guarantees nothing: proximity to a technology does not correlate that well with predicting its impact on society.

But they are the ones closest to it, and what they say deserves to be at least taken seriously. The rest of society, including some very intelligent people, has been far too quick to wave these scenarios away and not even get involved in the debate. Whether or not the belief is correct, it is sincerely held, and it is not “marketing hype.” I am writing this because I think it is high time that more people, inside San Francisco and out, engaged with the arguments about what our future will look like, and answered them.

text:
From addictive algorithms to exploitative apps, data mining to misinformation, the internet today can be a hazardous place. Books by three influential figures—the intellect behind “net neutrality,” a former Meta executive, and the web’s own inventor—propose radical approaches to fixing it. But are these luminaries the right people for the job? Though each shows conviction, and even sometimes inventiveness, the solutions they present reveal blind spots.

In The Age of Extraction: How Tech Platforms Conquered the Economy and Threaten Our Future Prosperity, Tim Wu argues that a few platform companies have too much concentrated power and must be dismantled. Wu, a prominent Columbia professor who popularized the principle that a free internet requires all online traffic to be treated equally, believes that existing legal mechanisms, especially anti-monopoly laws, offer the best way to achieve this goal.

Pairing economic theory with recent digital history, Wu shows how platforms have shifted from giving to users to extracting from them. He argues that our failure to understand their power has only encouraged them to grow, displacing competitors along the way. And he contends that convenience is what platforms most often exploit to keep users entrapped. “The human desire to avoid unnecessary pain and inconvenience,” he writes, may be “the strongest force out there.”

He cites Google’s and Apple’s “ecosystems” as examples, showing how users can become dependent on such services as a result of their all-­encompassing seamlessness. To Wu, this isn’t a bad thing in itself. The ease of using Amazon to stream entertainment, make online purchases, or help organize day-to-day life delivers obvious gains. But when powerhouse companies like Amazon, Apple, and Alphabet win the battle of convenience with so many users—and never let competitors get a foothold—the result is “industry dominance” that must now be reexamined.

The measures Wu advocates—and that appear the most practical, as they draw on existing legal frameworks and economic policies—are federal anti-monopoly laws, utility caps that limit how much companies can charge consumers for service, and “line of business” restrictions that prohibit companies from operating in certain industries.

Columbia University’s Tim Wu shows how platforms have shifted from giving to users to extracting from them. He argues that our failure to understand their power has only encouraged them to grow.

Anti-monopoly provisions and antitrust laws are effective weapons in our armory, Wu contends, pointing out that they have been successfully used against technology companies in the past. He cites two well-known cases. The first is the 1960s antitrust case brought by the US government against IBM, which helped create competition in the computer software market that enabled companies like Apple and Microsoft to emerge. The 1982 AT&T case that broke the telephone conglomerate up into several smaller companies is another instance. In each, the public benefited from the decoupling of hardware, software, and other services, leading to more competition and choice in a technology market.

But will past performance predict future results? It’s not yet clear whether these laws can be successful in the platform age. The 2025 antitrust case against Google—in which a judge ruled that the company did not have to divest itself of its Chrome browser as the US Justice Department had proposed—reveals the limits of pursuing tech breakups through the law. The 2001 antitrust case brought against Microsoft likewise failed to separate the company from its web browser and mostly kept the conglomerate intact. Wu noticeably doesn’t discuss the Microsoft case when arguing for antitrust action today.

Nick Clegg, until recently Meta’s president of global affairs and a former deputy prime minister of the UK, takes a position very different from Wu’s: that trying to break up the biggest tech companies is misguided and would degrade the experience of internet users. In How to Save the Internet: The Threat to Global Connection in the Age of AI and Political Conflict, Clegg acknowledges Big Tech’s monopoly over the web. But he believes punitive legal measures like antitrust laws are unproductive and can be avoided by means of regulation, such as rules for what content social media can and can’t publish. (It’s worth noting that Meta is facing its own antitrust case, involving whether it should have been allowed to acquire Instagram and WhatsApp.)

Clegg also believes Silicon Valley should take the initiative to reform itself. He argues that encouraging social media networks to “open up the books” and share their decision-making power with users is more likely to restore some equilibrium than contemplating legal action as a first resort.

But some may be skeptical of a former Meta exec and politician who worked closely with Mark Zuckerberg and still wasn’t able to usher in such changes to social media sites while working for one. What will only compound this skepticism is the selective history found in Clegg’s book, which briefly acknowledges some scandals (like the one surrounding Cambridge Analytica’s data harvesting from Facebook users in 2016) but refuses to discuss other pertinent ones. For example, Clegg laments the “fractured” nature of the global internet today but fails to acknowledge Facebook’s own role in this splintering.

Breaking up Big Tech through antitrust laws would hinder innovation, says Clegg, arguing that the idea “completely ignores the benefits users gain from large network effects.” Users stick with these outsize channels because they can find “most of what they’re looking for,” he writes, like friends and content on social media and cheap consumer goods on Amazon and eBay.

Wu might concede this point, but he would disagree with Clegg’s claims that maintaining the status quo is beneficial to users. “The traditional logic of antitrust law doesn’t work,” Clegg insists. Instead, he believes less sweeping regulation can help make Big Tech less dangerous while ensuring a better user experience.

Clegg has seen both sides of the regulatory coin: He worked in David Cameron’s government passing national laws for technology companies to follow and then moved to Meta to help the company navigate those types of nation-specific obligations. He bemoans the hassle and complexity Silicon Valley faces in trying to comply with differing rules across the globe, some set by “American federal agencies” and others by “Indian nationalists.”

But with the resources such companies command, surely they are more than equipped to cope? Given that Meta itself has previously meddled in access to the internet (such as in India, whose telecommunications regulator ultimately blocked its Free Basics internet service for violating net neutrality rules), this complaint seems suspect coming from Clegg. What should be the real priority, he argues, is not any new nation-specific laws but a global “treaty that protects the free flow of data between signatory countries.”

What the former Meta executive Nick Clegg advocates—unsurprisingly—is not a breakup of Big Tech but a push for it to become “radically transparent.”

Clegg believes that these nation-specific technology obligations—a recent one is Australia’s ban on social media for people under 16—usually reflect fallacies about the technology’s human impact, a subject that can be fraught with anxiety. Such laws have proved ineffective and tend to taint the public’s understanding of social networks, he says. There is some truth to his argument here, but reading a book in which a former Facebook executive dismisses techno-determinism—that is, the argument that technology makes people do or think certain things—may be cold comfort to those who have seen the harm technology can do.

In any case, Clegg’s defensiveness about social networks may not gain much favor from users themselves. He stresses the need for more personal responsibility, arguing that Meta doesn’t ever intend for users to stay on Facebook or Instagram endlessly: “How long you spend on the app in a single session is not nearly as important as getting you to come back over and over again.” Social media companies want to serve you content that is “meaningful to you,” he claims, not “simply to give you a momentary dopamine spike.” All this feels disingenuous at best.

What Clegg advocates—unsurprisingly—is not a breakup of Big Tech but a push for it to become “radically transparent,” whether on its own or, if necessary, with the help of federal legislators. He also wants platforms to bring users more into their governance processes (by using Facebook’s model of community forums to help improve their apps and products, for example). Finally, Clegg also wants Big Tech to give users more meaningful control of their data and how companies such as Meta can use it.

Here Clegg shares common ground with the inventor of the web, Tim Berners-Lee, whose own proposal for reform advances a technically specific vision for doing just that. In his memoir/manifesto This Is for Everyone: The Unfinished Story of the World Wide Web, Berners-Lee acknowledges that his initial vision—of a technology he hoped would remain open-source, collaborative, and completely decentralized—is a far cry from the web that we know today.

If there’s any surviving manifestation of his original project, he says, it’s Wikipedia, which remains “probably the best single example of what I wanted the web to be.” His best idea for moving power from Silicon Valley platforms into the hands of users is to give them more data control. He pushes for a universal data “pod” he helped develop, known as “Solid” (an abbreviation of “social linked data”).

The system—which was originally developed at MIT—would offer a central site where people could manage data ranging from credit card information to health records to social media comment history. “Rather than have all this stuff siloed off with different providers across the web, you’d be able to store your entire digital information trail in a single private repository,” Berners-Lee writes.

The Solid product may look like a kind of silver bullet in an age when data harvesting is familiar and data breaches are rampant. Placing greater control with users and enabling them to see “what data [i]s being generated about them” does sound like a tantalizing prospect.

But some people may have concerns about, for example, merging their confidential health records with data from personal devices (like heart rate info from a smart watch). No matter how much user control and decentralization Berners-Lee may promise, recent data scandals (such as cases in which period-tracking apps misused clients’ data) may be on people’s minds.

Berners-Lee believes that centralizing user data in a product like Solid could save people time and improve daily life on the internet. “An alien coming to Earth would think it was very strange that I had to tell my phone the same things again and again,” he complains about the experience of using different airline apps today.

With Solid, everything from vaccination records to credit card transactions could be kept within the digital vault and plugged into different apps. Berners-Lee believes that AI could also help people make more use of this data—for example, by linking meal plans to grocery bills. Still, if he’s optimistic on how AI and Solid could coordinate to improve users’ lives, he is vague on how to make sure that chatbots manage such personal data sensitively and safely.

Berners-Lee generally opposes regulation of the web (except in the case of teenagers and social media algorithms, where he sees a genuine need). He believes in internet users’ individual right to control their own data; he is confident that a product like Solid could “course-correct” the web from its current “exploitative” and extractive direction.

Of the three writers’ approaches to reform, it is Wu’s that has shown some effectiveness of late. Companies like Google have been forced to give competitors some advantage through data sharing, and they have now seen limits on how their systems can be used in new products and technologies. But in the current US political climate, will antitrust laws continue to be enforced against Big Tech?

Clegg may get his way on one issue: limiting new nation-specific laws. President Donald Trump has confirmed that he will use tariffs to penalize countries that ratify their own national laws targeting US tech companies. And given the posture of the Trump administration, it doesn’t seem likely that Big Tech will see more regulation in the US. Indeed, social networks have seemed emboldened (Meta, for example, removed fact-checkers and relaxed content moderation rules after Trump’s election win). In any case, the US hasn’t passed a major piece of federal internet legislation since 1996.

If using anti-monopoly laws through the courts isn’t possible, Clegg’s push for a US-led omnibus deal—setting consensual rules for data and acceptable standards of human rights—may be the only way to make some more immediate improvements.

text:
Rapid Refactoring with Claude: https://t.co/79u2UD2IfE

😱 Claude and I wrote our own long-running task runner for Tollbooth MCPs. This week, we ripped it out and replaced it in minutes.

❓Tollbooth DPYC MCPs needed an asynchronous Task Runner for long-running tool requests which need more time than the conventions of synchronous HTTP TCP requests will tolerate. For example, in eXcalibur, a service for generating X posts, a post can hold a dynamic block whose text is an LLM prompt. Resolving that block often takes minutes: the LLM model needs to survey the web, analyze responses, synthesize and compose marketing content, and returns professional "copy".

However, as is common in industry, the Tollbooth DPYC MCPs are deployed as on-demand, serverless instances. This infrastructure has demanding synchronous response deadlines and it recycles containers. Work started in the context of one request does not reliably outlive the request. (In fact, it reliably dies at the end of the request response.)

🛠️ So Claude and I built a deferred execution task runner service with tools for the client to specify jobs, check job status, and to claim finished jobs. The runtime sealed a job description with AES-256-GCM, shipped the ciphertext to a generic remote flow, and that flow interpreted a small vocabulary of operations. Results came back through the platform's artifact store, because its own result storage was the worker's local disk and unreadable from anywhere else. A per-operator secret block held the seal key. A non-secret selector rode in the clear so the shared flow could pick the right one.

It took seven rather complex concepts to move one function call out of the synchronous flow into an asynchronous runner.

Every one of these concepts existed for a defensible reason. The remote flow could not execute our code. So we invented a wire format and an interpreter to describe our code to it.

It worked - but...

💥 It also failed in ways that were hard to observe and diagnose. A dispatch error fell back to running in the calling MCP process, which looked healthy but was a fakeout. So, we responded by adding instrumentation. Then more instrumentation. Then instrumentation for the instrumentation. We got better at observing a tortured implementation rather than implementing a better solution. That's a code smell whose stink gets more and more intolerable.

🔎 Two announcements made us look up. Anthropic shipped Managed Agents. Deno released celld, self-hosted Durable Objects.

These are attractive - but, after consideration, neither fit.

❌ Managed Agents runs Claude only, and we route every model call through our choice of LLM provider using (rockstar) OpenRouter. Any technology that is wedded to Anthropic is a non-starter.

❌ celld and Cloudflare Workflows offer TypeScript language support - but not Python. Adopting them would mean having to have second implementations for our encryption services, as well as for any code that we would want to be able to run "in process" or via async runners. Two implementations of one algorithm is killer-drift just waiting to happen.

😁 Fortunately, these technologies did something better than just fitting: they inspired us to write each other the requirements for our capability, which we had never actually shared with each other (Claude and me). Those are:

- Accept a request synchronously.
- Allow running for tens to hundreds of minutes.
- Let the client come back later and claim the answer.
- Nothing in that path may be bound to a synchronous HTTP deadline.
- Support Python, because our operators are Python.
- Be Model agnostic.
- Require no new stateful infrastructure.
- Offer Per-operator isolation.

Stated clearly, the field of candidate solutions thinned quickly. (Which we kind of knew because that is why we started this by writing our own solution without doing really good research.)

Temporal, Hatchet, Restate, DBOS, Kitaru. All capable durable-execution engines. Supported by the Pydantic Team, too - very comforting.

But, every one of them still needs a worker or a cluster that we would have to self host or at least provision.

Kitaru came closest in spirit, with checkpoints and a wait() that releases compute to zero while even waiting for a human to participate in the flow. Really nice.

Kitaru's current available hosting targets are Kubernetes and the big clouds. We will keep watching it. Setting up a cluster is too much of a heavy-lift for Tollbooth DPYC Operators.

⚡ Modal won. It's the one that ran our code.

In Modal, a decorator annotation marks a function as runnable asynchronously. The method spawn() returns a handle in milliseconds. Functions can run up to twenty-four hours. Billing is per second and scales to zero. The handle can be redeemed from any process, which is precisely the claim check our tools already hand out.

(According to Claude) the refactoring in the MCPs was a mere three lines. Where the old code started a background task, the new code spawns. The determination about which requests need long-running that we had already written did not change at all. What changed is only where execution occurs.

👍 Deleting the obsolete code for our own runner removed 1,940 lines from the tollbooth-dpyc Python wheel. The runtime module alone lost 511. Gone: the sealed closure, the key selector, the per-operator secret block, the operation vocabulary, the interpreter flow, the artifact result channel, the result shaper.

The DRY elegance matters more than the line count. We had been maintaining two implementations of one resolution. One ran in process. The other was baked into a sealed specification for the remote interpreter, with a third function to translate its answers back. Same behaviour, three places to keep in step. Now there is one registration and one path.

🔑 The identity story is the part we like best.

The Modal container requires only one secret: the operator's Nostr nsec. From that it derives its npub, finds its Authority's configuration DM on a Nostr relay, and receives its database URL and its vault key. We copy no database URL. We copy no encryption key. The container ends up holding exactly what the MCP host holds, and the operator's human only ever handles the one value they already know (the nsec of their Operator).

We also looked at MCP Tasks, the emerging standard for starting a long call and polling it. In the 2026-07-28 release candidate it moved out of the core specification and became an extension after a redesign, and anyone who shipped against the earlier version has to migrate. We kept our own claim-check tools for now and will adopt the standard once it settles.

Economically, for pricing tools to Patron users, the toll fares did not change. The tools did not change. The Operator remains at liberty to set prices dynamically based on the infrastructure expenses for using Modal.

😎 eXcalibur's dynamic Posts stopped dying and our Observability headaches stopped flaring up.

⚡  With Tollbooth DPYC, your patrons purchase, out of band, tranches of "𝐴𝑃𝐼 𝑆𝑎𝑡𝑠", using rapid-settlement Lightning. Patrons then spend these API Sats across different tool calls with zero per-request friction and no KYC.

text:
Good morning India !

#ChhathPuja2026

A most awaited four day #ChhathPuja by the Hindus of #Bihar and #Jharkhand in India begins tomorrow, Friday November 13. Here are the details observed by me since my birth in Bihar:

Chhath (Hindi: #छठ, also called Dala Chhath) is an ancient Hindu Festival dedicated to the Sun God, known as #Surya. It is a festival observed most elaborately in Bihar and Jharkhand on the sixth day of the lunar month after Diwali every year, hence another name for Chhath is #SuryaShashti, usually a 4 day long celebration. In modern times it is also prevalent in areas where #migrants from Bihar and Jharkhand have a presence. Thus it is celebrated in all regions and major urban centers in India. Chhath is a way to be grateful to the Sun for giving the bounties of life on earth and for the fulfillment of wishes of believers. 

The four days Of Chhath Puja are as follows:

👉Day 1: "Nahay khay" Friday, November 13, 2026

On the first day of Chhath Puja, the devotees take a dip, preferably in the holy river #Ganga and carry home the holy water of Ganga to prepare the offerings. The house and surroundings are scrupulously cleaned. The ladies observing the fast (#vrat) known in Hindi as #Vratins allow themselves only one meal on this day.

👉Day 2: "Kharna" (the day before Chhath) 

Saturday, November 14, 2026

On the day before Chhath, the #Vratins observe a fast for the whole day, which ends in the evening a little after sunset. Just after the worship of Sun, the offerings of #rasiaokheer (rice delicacy), #puris (deep-fried puffs of wheat flour) and bananas are distributed among  the family and friends. The next 👉36 hours, the Vratins go on a 👉fast without water.

Day 3: 👉Chhath 

Sunday November 15, 2026

#SanjhiyaArghya (evening offerings): The day is spent preparing the #prasadam (offerings) at home. On the eve of this day, the entire household accompanies the Vratins to a riverbank, pond or a common large water body to offer #Arghya to the setting sun. It is during this phase of Chhath Puja that the devotees offer prayers to the just setting sun. The occasion is almost a carnival. Besides the Vratins, there are friends and family, and numerous participants and onlookers, all willing to help and receive the blessings of the worshipper. The folk songs sung on the evening of Chhath reflect the culture, social structure, mythology and history of Bihar and Jharkhand. The three main linguistic regions of Bihar (the #Maithili, the #Magadhi, and the #Bhojpuri), and all the various dialects associated with these, have different folk songs; but have an underlying unity in their dedication to Chhath.

👉Day 4: "Paarun" (the day after Chhath) 

Monday November 16, 2026

#BihaniyaArghya (next morning offerings): On the final day of Chhath Puja, the devotees, along with family and friends, go to the riverbank before sunrise, in order to make the offerings (Arghya) to the rising sun. The festival ends with the breaking of the fast by the Vratins and friends visiting the houses of the devotees to receive the #prasadam . 

The chhath has so much importance that even millionaires beg for prasadam at the #Chhathghat. This symbolizes that all persons are beggars in front of the Almighty.

👉Why Salutations to the Setting Sun ?

Chhath is the only time in Hinduism when the setting sun as opposed to its rising is celebrated for its glory because according to the theory of #reincarnation deeply rooted in Hinduism, the cycle of birth starts with death.

🌹 THE ROSETO EFFECT —
WHAT DEATH CERTIFICATES CAN'T COUNT, AND WHAT AMERICA IS LETTING GO 🫀

— A Special Investigation
In 1964, JAMA put heart attack deaths in Roseto, Pa., at under half the rate of nearby towns. After 1965 the gap closed. Did the town's closeness protect it?

✍️ By 3 Star Media — The BX Files 🏇💨

Around 1961, Roseto was a borough of about 1,600 people on a hillside in eastern Pennsylvania's Slate Belt, with the larger town of Bangor directly beside it. Its main street was Garibaldi Avenue. Its stone church, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, had stood since 1923, and the Marconi Club had been meeting since 1903.

The slate quarries had drawn the first families, and blouse factories had since joined them as employers. Nearly half the households still made their own wine. Almost everyone in town traced back to a single village in southern Italy.

It was an ordinary working town in a country with a heart problem. Heart disease had been the leading cause of death in the United States since 1921, and coronary death rates were still climbing. In 1961 the American Heart Association advised that cutting saturated fat might help prevent heart attacks.

In that climate a local physician, Dr. Benjamin Falcone, made a remark to a visiting researcher. He said he rarely saw a heart attack in anyone there under 65.

The visitor was Stewart Wolf, head of the Department of Medicine at the University of Oklahoma, who had founded a research laboratory at Totts Gap, outside Bangor, in 1958. Wolf had made his name recording what stress did to one patient's stomach.

🎯 THE KEY QUESTION What was protecting the hearts of Roseto, and was anything protecting them at all?

▸ ▸ ▸

The town was an accident of a labor market.

Its first settlers came in 1882 from Roseto Valfortore, a hill town in the province of Foggia, to cut slate in a district settled mostly by people of Welsh, English and German descent. They built on the hill above Bangor and named the place for home.

The borough's own history fills in what they built next. The first July celebration for Our Lady of Mount Carmel, known as the Big Time, came in 1895. Father Pasquale De Nisco arrived in 1897 as the first resident priest. He pushed parents to send their children to school, prepared hundreds of people for citizenship, and directed a strike that the borough says lifted daily pay from 85 cents to $1.50.

On Jan. 2, 1912, a county judge approved Roseto's incorporation.

Roseto's closeness was not a mood. It was a set of institutions, built over decades: a parish, a union, clubs, a festival and a government of its own.

▸ ▸ ▸

Wolf's team set up a clinic in Roseto in December 1962 and came back the next two summers, examining Rosetans and their relatives. They also went through seven years of local death records.

The result ran in the Journal of the American Medical Association on June 8, 1964, with Clarke Stout as lead author. From 1955 through 1961, Roseto's death rate from myocardial infarction, the medical term for a heart attack, was less than half that of the surrounding communities. The gap showed in both sexes and was widest among men. No one under 47 had died of a heart attack in those seven years.

Each obvious explanation was tried, and each came up short.

Diet was the first to go. Men ate about 3,000 calories a day and 41 percent of Rosetans' calories came from fat, by the team's figures. Olive oil was the lesser oil in the kitchen. Years later Wolf described a favorite local dish to a room of physicians: peppers fried in lard, with bread to wipe up what was left.

Habits explained no more. About as many Rosetans smoked as their neighbors, and they were at least as heavy. Men averaged about 34 grams of alcohol a day, roughly three glasses of wine, a figure the wine science journal OENO One drew from the team's work in a 2024 review. The team could find no difference in exercise between the towns.

Heredity looked unlikely. Relatives living elsewhere showed more signs of heart disease, the team reported, and several Roseto-born men who had spent their lives in other towns died of heart attacks before 45.

Nor was it the place. Bangor drew on the same water supply, the same physicians and the same hospital.

The 1964 paper did not claim an answer. Whether Rosetans owed their luck to their way of life or to genetic or ethnic factors, it said, "remains to be determined." What it did say is that in this one town, obesity and plenty of calories, fat and wine sat alongside a strikingly low heart attack death rate.

💡 The bottom line: in the first paper, community was not the finding. It was the last suspect left in the room.

▸ ▸ ▸

The sociologist John Bruhn had joined the project to look at what a medical exam could not see.

What the team recorded was a particular kind of town. Most households held three generations. People bought from local shops and married mostly within the group, and in the evening they walked the town, visiting with neighbors.

The wealthy did not show it. A young Italian anthropologist working in the town traced that to an old village belief about the evil eye: children were taught that any display of superiority over a neighbor brought bad luck.

From this the team built a hypothesis. A stable town where a person was never without family, a role or help might blunt the wear of chronic stress, and a heart under less strain might last longer.

The team had counted structures: households, marriages, memberships. The feeling those structures were supposed to produce, the sense that someone would show up, was inferred.

The biology behind the idea is real. A perceived threat raises heart rate and blood pressure and starts a hormonal chain that ends in cortisol, and kept up for years that response is associated with higher blood pressure and chronic inflammation.

⚠️ None of that was measured in Roseto. The pathway makes the hypothesis plausible. It does not show that this is what happened on Garibaldi Avenue.

A town where most people marry inside the group and nobody shows off is a picture of belonging, and also of pressure. The record does not say what that cost someone who did not fit, and that silence reflects who was asked, not proof the cost was zero.

▸ ▸ ▸

The researchers saw the change coming. In interviews, Rosetans under 35 voiced respect for the old ways and no wish to live by them.

The team predicted that if those ways went, the protection would go with them. Its own accounts disagree on when. A 1989 report says the prediction was "made and recorded" in 1963, and a 1974 report places it after a 1965 survey of the town.

Then the old Roseto came apart, and the team's reports list how. Expensive cars appeared. Families left the close-set houses for ranch homes at the edge of town and drove to supermarkets elsewhere, and local shops closed. People joined country clubs, and attendance fell at the men's clubs and the church.

Between 1960 and 1980 the population fell 8 percent while the number of households rose 8 percent. Elderly Rosetans, once cared for at home, entered nursing homes. By 1985 the evening walk was "hardly observed at all."

Nobody in Roseto was punished for wanting more schooling, a wider world or a spouse from the next town. Those were gains. Fewer than 10 percent of Rosetans had finished high school in 1940, and 65 percent had by 1980.

▸ ▸ ▸

The deaths moved with the town. From 1962 to 1965 no Rosetan under 55 died of a heart attack. By 1970, men and women in Roseto were dying of heart attacks at more than twice the rate recorded for 1955 through 1961.

In the first half of 1971, two men between 35 and 44 died of heart attacks, the first in that age group in more than 16 years of study. The team wrote up both. Each had lived outside the town's social life, and one had told an interviewer five years earlier, "I don't fit in the town."

Two cases chosen after the fact prove nothing, and the team did not claim they did. Both men were also heavy smokers, and each had a parent who died of a heart attack. Its 1974 report said that because the numbers were small, "statistical significance cannot be attached" to Roseto's rising rate. Wolf told his colleagues that 16 years of data had "pretty well disposed of" the skepticism about small numbers.

The same report held one hard number. Across all 16 years, heart attack deaths before 65 in Roseto and Bangor differed at a level it called highly significant, with odds of chance under one in 1,000. The team itself had sorted those deaths, including heart attacks it classed as presumed.

Two researchers at Lehigh University's Center for Social Research, Brenda Egolf and Judith Lasker, joined Wolf and Louise Potvin of the University of Montreal to find out whether the whole thing had been a fluke. Their stated worry was that in a town this small, the gap might be "random fluctuations."

They examined 3,859 death certificates for Roseto and Bangor covering 1935 to 1985, checked them against obituaries and church records, and adjusted for age. The study ran in the American Journal of Public Health in August 1992.

Over the 30 years from 1935 to 1964, Roseto's heart attack death rate was significantly lower than Bangor's, in men and in women. After 1965 the difference disappeared. The authors called the earlier gap "statistically significant despite the small number of myocardial infarctions."

Two details in that paper cut against the fluke theory. The certificates from 1935 through the 1950s were filled out before anyone was studying the town. And the rise did not look like simple aging. Among women it came entirely at 65 and older, but among men it reached every age group and hit hardest under 65.

The study has limits too. Wolf, whose hypothesis was on trial, was one of its four authors. The paper does not say whether the people sorting certificates knew which town each came from. It compares two towns, not individuals, so it cannot show that the Rosetans with the strongest ties were the ones who lived.

🔍 What the evidence shows: Roseto's rate rose as the nation's began to fall.

U.S. coronary death rates peaked in the 1960s and then began a decline that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counts among the great public health achievements of the century.

◆ ◆ ◆

The strongest case against the Roseto Effect was made almost at once.

Ancel Keys, the Minnesota physiologist behind the theory that saturated fat drives heart disease, answered in JAMA in January 1966. An electrocardiogram survey, he wrote, gave no support to the idea that Rosetans were protected. The death data for 1955 to 1961 did not show them differing significantly from average white Americans.

Keys added that the Rosetans' earlier diet should have given them some protection, and that the town may have been too small to show even that. Nothing, he concluded, supported crediting the town's emotional climate.

The team felt the pressure. Wolf said it had studied the Roseto diet so elaborately because it had Keys "breathing down our necks." Keys had a stake too, because a town eating this much fat was a problem for his theory. That does not make him wrong about the arithmetic.

The modern version comes from three researchers at New York University, Samrachana Adhikari, Olugbenga Ogedegbe and Orrin Devinsky. It was posted as a preprint in 2024 and published in the journal Cureus in July 2026.

They took heart attack death rates from the Framingham Heart Study, which they call the only American population with comparable data from those years, and simulated what a town of Roseto's size should expect. Roseto's deaths from 1955 to 1964 fell inside the expected range at every age but one. At 65 and over, Roseto did worse.

Their other points are harder to wave off. Only 62 Roseto men were aged 55 to 64, too few to carry a finding. Bangor may have been a sick neighbor: its men over 45 died of cardiovascular disease at more than four times the Framingham rate.

Here the two sides collide. The team reported 1 heart attack death per 1,000 Roseto men from 1955 to 1961 against a national 3.5, and said the neighboring towns ran near the national figure. The NYU team says the neighbor was the outlier. Both cannot be right.

Wolf did not pick Roseto at random. He was told it was special and then went to look.

Roseto men also had far less diabetes, 26 cases per 1,000 against 44 in Nazareth and 94 in Bangor. That alone could move a town's heart deaths, though Roseto women had more diabetes than women in Nazareth. No death data followed the men who moved away. And the people gathering the data knew the story: by the team's 1974 report, a local physician supplied the family circumstances of each death from 1966 to 1970, the years the rise appeared.

Their conclusion is that the Roseto study "neither supported nor refuted" a link between social support and heart health.

That critique has gaps of its own. The published paper cites the 1992 death certificate study only for Roseto's population counts and never takes up its 30-year finding. It offers no account of why Roseto's rate rose after 1965.

One finding in the 1992 paper does not depend on how any doctor labeled a death. Counting deaths from all causes, Roseto men died at significantly lower rates than Bangor men in four of the five decades, including the last one, after the old Roseto was gone. Roseto women ran lower than Bangor women in two decades and significantly higher in 1965 to 1974. Those facts are awkward for the critics and for the believers alike.

Most of the usual suspects do not explain the rise. By the team's 1989 report, Rosetans were eating less animal fat and lard than in 1963, fewer of the men smoked, and cholesterol had not changed. Exercise had dropped, but it had dropped in the neighboring towns as well.

One suspect stays. High blood pressure rose sharply in Roseto, to nearly Bangor's level, and strokes more than doubled. The team read that as part of the stress story, but it is a conventional risk factor all the same. Who moved in and out was never tested, and neither was the decline of the quarries and blouse factories.

The order of events is unsettled as well. The team dates the first cracks in the old customs to the middle and late 1960s, at the turn or after it, not clearly before. Its 1994 companion study says the social changes sped up in the 1960s and that this "coincided with and may help to explain" the loss. The 1989 report's own wording is that the link is "likely, but by no means certain."

📊 For 30 years, death certificates recorded fewer fatal heart attacks in Roseto than in the town next door, and after 1965 they stopped doing so.

⚖️ Whether Roseto was ever unusual beside the country as a whole is disputed. On that question the small numbers favor Keys and the NYU team, and one small town cannot settle it.

❌ That the town's closeness caused the gap has not been established. The two changed together in one place, and that is a correlation.

▸ ▸ ▸

Roseto is no longer the evidence the idea stands on. What came after is.

🔒 Five different things get blurred in this debate, and each study measures only some of them.

Loneliness is a feeling. Perceived support is a belief, the sense that someone would show up. Isolation is a count of contacts. Integration is the number of roles and groups a person holds.

Cohesion is the fifth, and it belongs to a place, not a person.

In 2010, Julianne Holt-Lunstad and colleagues pooled 148 studies following 308,849 people and found that those with stronger social relationships had a 50 percent greater likelihood of surviving the follow-up period. In 2016, a team led by Nicole Valtorta pooled long-term studies and tied poor social relationships to a 29 percent higher risk of coronary heart disease and a 32 percent higher risk of stroke.

⚠️ Those are associations. A 2022 scientific statement from the American Heart Association, led by Crystal Cené, called the link consistent but warned that "the effect estimates are small" and that unmeasured factors may be at work. It also pointed to a lack of data on whether easing isolation or loneliness improves heart health.

The closest thing to an experiment is sobering. The ENRICHD trial, published in JAMA in 2003, enrolled 2,481 people who had just had a heart attack and were depressed, short on social support, or both. Cognitive behavioral therapy, with antidepressants when needed, improved their mood and their support scores. Over an average of 29 months, death or a second heart attack came to 24.2 percent of the treated group and 24.1 percent of the rest.

ENRICHD tested the second thing on that list, in people who were already sick. The feeling improved and the hearts did not. Roseto's hypothesis is mostly about the fifth, and by the heart association's review, the trials that would test it have not been done.

None of that erases the link between isolation and early death. It means the link has not yet been turned into a treatment.

▸ ▸ ▸

Set the Roseto team's checklist beside the United States of 2026 and the direction is hard to miss.

Start with households. In 2025, 29 percent of American households were one person living alone, the Census Bureau reported, against 20 percent in 1975.

Time has moved the same way. On an average day in 2025, 30 percent of Americans 15 and older spent any time socializing and communicating, down from 38 percent in 2015, by the Bureau of Labor Statistics survey released in June 2026. The share was 34.8 percent in 2019 and 29.1 percent in 2021, and it has not come back.

So have the institutions. Seventy percent of Americans belonged to a church, synagogue or mosque in 1999 and 47 percent did in 2020, the first reading below half in Gallup's eight decades of asking.

In June 2025 the World Health Organization's Commission on Social Connection reported that about one person in six worldwide is affected by loneliness, and estimated that it is linked to some 871,000 deaths a year.

The drift is not uniform. Multigenerational living, one of the traits the Roseto team counted, has been rising for 50 years. Seven percent of Americans lived in such homes in 1971 and 18 percent did in 2021, by Pew Research Center's count.

The feeling has not tracked the structures either. Gallup's daily loneliness reading was 20 percent in late summer 2024, below the 25 percent it recorded in March 2021. In 2019 the researcher Esteban Ortiz-Ospina of Our World in Data reviewed long-running surveys and found no clear evidence that loneliness itself had been rising.

🔍 What the evidence shows: the structures are thinning faster than the feeling is rising.

That is the part of the story Roseto speaks to. Its researchers never measured how lonely anyone felt. They counted households, marriages, memberships and where people shopped, and those are the measures now moving across the country.

Roseto's young told the researchers they wanted the life of the towns around them. Today's drift travels with the same things: mobility, schooling and the freedom to choose. Few people would hand those back, and no one should be asked to.

What would change the direction is not an order to go make friends. The surgeon general's advisory points at the settings that make ordinary contact easy, such as parks, libraries and public transit. Those are reasonable bets, not findings.

◆ ◆ ◆

Roseto had 1,581 residents at the 2020 census, about what it had when Wolf arrived. The borough's history page lists what remains on Garibaldi Avenue: a barber shop, a restaurant and a bakery. The Big Time is still held.

On Fridays in Lent, the fire company serves dinner by reservation, and in March 2024 The Philadelphia Inquirer counted 230 bookings for one night. A 78-year-old woman who grew up with the firemen doing the cooking told the paper, "This is Roseto. It's how we show love."

Wolf moved to Pennsylvania in 1978 to spend more time studying Roseto, by the National Library of Medicine's account. He died in 2005, at 91, without a controlled answer.

What he left is a file. Fifty years of death certificates can say what stopped each heart in Roseto. Not one has a line for who was in the house, or who came to the door. Whatever medicine decides about this town, it is still learning how to count that.

A note on sources: this report draws on the original Roseto papers in JAMA and the American Journal of Public Health and on the research team's own reports of 1974 and 1989; a 2026 critique read in its published form; obituaries from medical institutions and journals; the borough's own history; federal census, time use and mortality data; pooled analyses and one clinical trial; and news reporting. Three original texts sit behind paywalls and are cited through their abstracts, as the text says where it matters.

text:
A thought on God and existential risk that came up in a lunchtime conversation today:

In the episode of The Argument Podcast where @mattyglesias and @JerusalemDemsas discuss AI existential risk, Jerusalem argues that people worried about AI-driven human extinction should avoid talking about that and instead focus on policies that alleviate sub-extinction-level risks, since these are a bit easier to wrap one's mind around.

(Matt responds that this might be true in some cases, but we don't really know that the same policies would work for both. I agree with this, and also think we should be honest about the stakes because they imply a different level of appropriate urgency.)

Then, about 45 minutes into the episode, Matt speculates that religious people might have "a little bit of complacency about truly epic catastrophe." (Later, he notes that people in the 1980s thought Reagan was too blithe about the risks of nuclear war for similar reasons.)

Jerusalem's response, I think, puts her previous arguments in a different light:

"I will cop to this. I definitely think that my religious beliefs make me unwilling to believe that this is going to happen."

I'm not an expert in any theology, and I'm not going to argue with anyone's faith. (I'm also not religious, and I recognize secular people often aren't persuasive when they talk in religious terms.)

But I think that is the wrong way to think about it, because of the following modern parable I first encountered (in a slightly different form) in David Foster Wallace's This Is Water speech:

A man is stranded on his roof during a 100-year flood. After a while, someone in a rowboat comes by and offers him a seat. He says: "No, God will save me."

After a few more hours, another man pulls up in a motorboat and throws him a rope. He says: "Don't need it, God will save me."

The next morning, as he gets thirstier and hungrier, a helicopter comes by and lowers a ladder. He says: "No thanks, God will save me."

He passes away, and when in heaven, angrily asks God: "I waited so long! Why didn't you save me?"

God says: "I sent you two boats and a helicopter."

The closest the actual Bible gets to making this point comes from Jesus's temptation, when Satan tells Jesus to jump from the top of the temple, quoting Psalm 91: "He will command his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone."

Jesus quotes back: "It is also written: 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test.'"

(There's also Nehemiah 4:9: "But we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night to meet this threat.")

In the case of AI extinction, I think having faith in God must not mean we jump off the temple. We must post a guard day and night; we must accept whatever boats and helicopters come our way.

So, I won't tell Jerusalem she shouldn't have faith that we will make it in the end. But I do think our own actions, and our policy responses, must take the responsibility of prevention very seriously, because those are the very mechanisms by which I think we will avert catastrophe.

As Kennedy said in his inaugural, "Let us go forth to lead the land we love, asking His blessing and His help, but knowing that here on earth God's work must truly be our own."

TEXAS ROADHOUSE IS PUTTING CHICKEN ALFREDO IN 700 RESTAURANTS. THEIR OWN INVESTOR RELATIONS GUY ADMITS NOBODY WILL ORDER IT. 🥩

It's in more than 600 locations already, with the last hundred coming by spring. They announced this on an earnings call, out loud, on purpose.

Michael Bailen, VP of investor relations, on the record: the pasta is "probably not going to be one of our top 10 mix entree items that we offer, but it rounds out the menu."

Sir. You just described a dish nobody wants, going into seven hundred buildings.

Somebody on Reddit asked the only question that matters. "Who goes to a steakhouse and orders chicken Alfredo?" Nobody. That's the answer.

Please do not turn into Olive Garden. I've had the lobster carbonara there. It's a can of SpaghettiOs in a tuxedo, sitting next to breadsticks engineered to fill you up before the entree lands.

And since we're here, let me tell you what Alfredo is, because almost nobody in this country has eaten it.

A Roman cook named Alfredo di Lelio made it around 1908 for his wife Ines, who had just had a baby and would not eat. Three things. Fresh fettuccine, young butter, Parmigiano Reggiano. You build the sauce by hand, tossing hot pasta with butter and cheese and a splash of starchy water until it goes glossy. No cream. No flour. No garlic. No chicken, not then, not ever. Italians don't even call it Alfredo. It's fettuccine al burro.

Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks ate there in the twenties, came home raving, and we had it wrecked inside a decade. Cream first. Then a roux. Then chicken.

What comes off a steam table here isn't a variation on anything. It's the lunch lady version and it should be banned.

The penne has nothing to do with cooking, by the way. It's a hedge.

Our cattle herd is down to 86.2 million head, smallest since 1951. The breeding cows that decide what gets slaughtered three years out sit at 27.6 million, lowest since 1961. Ground beef cleared $6.70 a pound this spring and nobody expects relief before 2028. The company told investors to plan on 4% commodity inflation next year, half of it beef.

Chicken and pasta cost a fraction of a ribeye. So the hedge got a press release.

The business under all this is soft. Sales rose 4.3% last quarter, but the check did the work and traffic moved seven tenths of a percent. September came in at 1%.

Some of that September drop was not their fault, and this part is not funny. A hoax went around social media claiming Texas Roadhouse employees planned to tamper with Black customers' food. The company ran forensics on it. It was a lie. People shared it anyway, and hourly workers in seven hundred towns ate the tip shortage.

So here's my suggestion, free of charge. You named yourself after my state. Act like it.

Serve more pig. Beef hit $9.64 a pound this spring, a record, up 13% in a year. Pork chops ran $4.33 and barely budged. You already make ribs people drive across town for, pork costs about half the protein your whole name rides on, and everybody loves the magical animal. Ham steak. Thick cut chops. A tenderloin. Bacon in mountain form. Call the section the Javelina Plate and charge me eighteen dollars.

Then put Texas Gulf shrimp on it. Roughly 94% of the shrimp Americans eat is imported, mostly farmed overseas, while shrimpers out of Brownsville and Port Isabel run boats at a loss. Texas declared a disaster over it. Seven hundred restaurants buying Gulf-caught moves real money to real Americans, and it beats anything thawed out of a bag.

While we're being candid, you're headquartered in Louisville and your first store opened in Clarksville, Indiana. You have been selling Texas to America for thirty three years on vibes alone. Lean in. Earn the name.

The herd doesn't come back until 2028. Keep the rolls free, raise the steak four bucks and tell me why, and leave the penne alone. If I want fettuccine I'll make it in my own kitchen, with butter and cheese, and I'm not adding chicken either. 🦋

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐞: 𝐄𝐥𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐮𝐬𝐤'𝐬 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫.
Something rather extraordinary is happening in the technology industry, and I suspect most people have barely noticed.

Elon Musk's SpaceX has formally applied to the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for permission to deploy up to one million satellites that will function as orbital data centres.

Yes, data centres in space.

And when you understand how the system is intended to work, you begin to appreciate why this could have enormous implications for the future of computing.

Why move computers into orbit?

The biggest problem facing the expansion of artificial intelligence is no longer simply the availability of computer chips. It is the infrastructure needed to operate them.

Modern data centres consume enormous amounts of electricity, require substantial cooling systems, compete for land and place increasing demands on water supplies and electricity grids.

Musk's proposal attempts to remove many of these constraints.

Instead of building enormous facilities on Earth, SpaceX wants to put computing satellites into orbit, where they can collect solar energy directly.

The proposed satellites would operate between 500 and 2,000 kilometres above Earth, using high-speed optical laser connections to communicate with one another and with the existing Starlink network.

Think of it as thousands, potentially millions, of computers operating together in space, forming an enormous distributed computing network.

Where does the electricity come from?

The Sun.

In carefully selected orbits, satellites can receive sunlight for almost the entire day, avoiding many of the interruptions experienced by conventional solar installations on Earth.

Large solar arrays would generate the electricity needed to operate the computing equipment.

There would be no requirement to connect to a terrestrial electricity grid, no coal-fired power stations and no competition with households and industries for electricity.

And what about cooling?

This is one of the most interesting engineering aspects.

Space is a vacuum, so conventional air cooling and water cooling cannot work in the usual way.

However, heat can be transferred from processors into aluminium structures and then released through large radiator panels as infrared radiation.

The system would use passive radiative cooling rather than conventional water-intensive cooling towers and refrigeration systems.

It is not as simple as putting a computer outside in the cold, but it offers an entirely different approach to thermal management.

The really extraordinary idea: manufacturing on the Moon

Musk has also discussed something that sounds like science fiction.

He wants to establish manufacturing facilities on the Moon, potentially producing solar panels, radiators and computing satellites using lunar resources.

Then comes the remarkable part.

Instead of using rockets to launch every satellite, he has proposed building an enormous electromagnetic catapult, known as a mass driver.

The Moon has only one-sixth of Earth's gravity and virtually no atmosphere.

An electromagnetic launcher could accelerate manufactured components to sufficient speeds to send them into space without conventional chemical rockets.

The electronics and other components that cannot initially be manufactured on the Moon could still be transported there from Earth.

It is an ambitious long-term vision, not an approved construction project, but the underlying engineering concept is real.

Is this actually happening?

SpaceX's application for up to one million orbital data-centre satellites was accepted for consideration by the FCC in February 2026.

This is not simply a social media announcement. It is a formal regulatory proposal.

Other companies are also investigating orbital computing, but SpaceX has an enormous advantage through its existing satellite network, launch capability and manufacturing infrastructure.

There are significant challenges ahead, including radiation, maintenance, orbital debris, launch costs and the enormous radiator surfaces required to remove heat.

Nobody should mistake a regulatory application for a completed technology.

But consider what this could mean.

No enormous buildings occupying valuable land.

No water-intensive cooling infrastructure.

No dependence on local electricity grids.

No conventional rocket launches forever, if lunar manufacturing and electromagnetic launch eventually become practical.

And potentially an enormous computing network powered directly by the Sun.

We have spent decades building bigger and bigger computer facilities on Earth. We may now be approaching a point where the most economical place to build the next generation of computing infrastructure is above our heads.

The data centre of the future might not be a building at all.

It might be orbiting the planet.

And that is a development worth paying attention to.

Ole Miss "Racial Incident" Victims Admit Girls Claimed They Hit Four Other Doors: "We Didn't Mean Any Harm"

The media rushed to frame a November 6 Ring camera clip at Ole Miss as a clear-cut case of targeted racial harassment. Three white female students walked past an off-campus apartment housing Black freshmen, and two of them—Alaina Kunes and another woman—beat their chests and made ape-like noises toward the camera. One has since withdrawn from the university amid threats. University officials condemned the "racist gestures" and opened an investigation.

But the Black students who live there, Jakirya Metcalf and Victoria Johnson, told CBS that when they immediately went outside to confront the group, one of the girls apologized on the spot and offered a different explanation.

Metcalf said: "We actually went outside and tried to like approach them and like have them get them to like explain why they did that. One girl was apologizing. She was like, I'm sorry, we did that to like four doors. And mind you, we didn't see anyone else do it. It was just ours that was targeted. And she was like, we didn't mean any harm."

The students maintain they only saw the behavior at their door and felt targeted. They also said the second woman kept making the gestures even while the first was apologizing, which Metcalf called "like a slap in the face."

Metcalf added that she told them the behavior was disrespectful regardless: "Yeah, I had said that I don't think they should go around, even if they did go to other people's door and do that, I don't think they should do that because it's very disrespectful."

Kunes later issued a public statement: "To the women I offended and to the Ole Miss community, I sincerely apologize. Before the incident on November 6, I never met the women involved and was unaware of their race. However, I recognize my actions were insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful. I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color. I have apologized to the women, and I pray they will forgive me."

Asked if she forgives her, Metcalf said she has "mixed feelings" and that the gestures and noises were "very disrespectful" no matter whether the girls knew their race.

Johnson said: "I appreciate the apology, but I feel like it still doesn't change what happened on that Friday, because it's still hurtful and it's still devastating that someone would come to our camera and do that."

text:
"A young girl with SCID becomes an advocate for herself and others"

A must read story for all.

Seersha Sulack’s story is an inspiration for families affected by ‘bubble baby disease.’

By Nicole Chien | Jun 23, 2025 Patient Stories
This article was originally published by UCLA Health
Seersha Sulack’s childhood has been anything but ordinary.

For the first five years of her life, hospital rooms replaced playgrounds. Doctor visits took the place of playdates. Weekly injections became all too familiar. And avoiding exposure to germs always took priority.

Just days after birth, Seersha was diagnosed with ADA-SCID (adenosine deaminase-deficient severe combined immunodeficiency) — a rare genetic condition, also known as “bubble baby disease,” that impairs the immune systems of children.

Despite the constraints of her early life, Seersha remained driven by resilience and ambition. Now, at just 7 years old, she is a fearless self-advocate.

“Seersha is a firecracker. She speaks her mind and is really sweet,” says Donald Kohn, MD, a member of the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research at UCLA.

“Her energy is always up,” her mother, Shayla Sulack, adds. “She’s never met a stranger that she didn’t become friends with.”

That energy lit up Dodger Stadium on May 17, when Seersha was surprised with the opportunity to throw out the ceremonial first pitch and meet her favorite baseball player, Mookie Betts.

As she approached the pitcher’s mound and danced with excitement, Seersha was fulfilling a dream many would have thought impossible after her diagnosis.

Blood sample tells the story
Seersha was born Oct. 21, 2017, in a military hospital in Honolulu, Hawaii, the third child of the Sulack family.

The family’s jubilation quickly dimmed, however, when a routine blood test — including a standard SCID screening administered for all newborns in the U.S. — raised concern. A geneticist at the hospital discovered Seersha lacked T cells, a primary indicator of SCID.

With specialized expertise unavailable locally, the sample was sent to UCLA Health, a nationally recognized leader in immunodeficiency care, for further analysis. There, Manish Butte, MD, PhD, chief of Immunology, Allergy, and Rheumatology, conducted additional testing and confirmed Seersha’s SCID diagnosis.

At just 6 days old, Seersha was airlifted to Los Angeles on a military medical transport flight alongside her mother. To minimize her exposure, she was placed in an incubator at the front of the plane.

“It was terrifying to leave my husband and two other children not knowing when they were going to see her again. We had no idea what we were doing,” says Shayla Sulack, reflecting on the early days of treatment. The entire family eventually relocated to Tehachapi to be closer to Seersha’s UCLA Health team and relatives in the area.

Seersha’s parents feared their youngest child would not make it to her first birthday, but Dr. Kohn’s groundbreaking work in gene therapy — to repair the immune systems of children with SCID — would soon offer hope.

Treatment options for severe combined immunodeficiency disease

According to Dr. Kohn, Seersha inherited two faulty copies of the gene responsible for producing adenosine deaminase, or ADA, a critical enzyme needed by T cells to survive.

“We had no idea we were carriers until we had Seersha,” says Shayla Sulack.

Dr. Kohn and his team leveraged their expertise and explored different treatment options.

“Before treatments existed, SCID was uniformly a fatal disease in infancy. Babies would die within the first year of life from infections,” Dr. Kohn says. “Fortunately, today, that is no longer the case.”

There are two main treatment pathways for children with SCID: bone marrow transplant and gene therapy. Both treatments offer a potential cure, but each comes with unique risks and benefits.

Bone marrow transplants involve the transfer of healthy stem cells from a compatible donor — typically a family member — to the patient.

“If there is a sibling who is a perfect match and does not have SCID, then the chance of a successful transplant is 90-95%,” says Dr. Kohn.

However, this ideal scenario is relatively rare. With only a 25% chance that two siblings will be a perfect match, this option is not viable for many patients. That was the case for Seersha.

“When we first arrived at UCLA, we got our HLA typing done,” explains Seersha’s mom. “My husband and I were only half matches, and our older children were not matches for her at all.”

In these cases, doctors may need to look beyond immediate family. “We can either use the parent who’s half a match, or we can look for an unrelated donor,” explains Dr. Kohn.

But while 80%-90% of children survive these unrelated or half-matched bone marrow transplants, the procedures are often associated with higher risks, including graft-versus-host disease — where donor cells attack the patient.

As a result, to provide Seersha with her best chance for a cure, Dr. Kohn offered the family an alternative: gene therapy.

A unique approach to SCID
Gene therapy involves the process of removing a patient’s stem cells, correcting their genetic makeup, and reintroducing the cells back into the body. In clinical trials administered by Dr. Kohn and his team, gene therapy at UCLA Health has saved the lives of more than 50 babies to date.

“We like gene therapy for us, because we didn’t have to worry about rejection, graft-versus-host disease or anything else. If it didn’t work, we could do other options,” explains Shayla Sulack. “The doctors were also really great about explaining this to Seersha. Because at the end of the day, she's the one living with it, and we're just taking care of it.”

Dr. Kohn and his team extracted Seersha’s stem cells and inserted a normal ADA gene into them. They used a virus as a carrier to deliver the corrected gene into her DNA and reintroduced the modified cells back into her body.

“If gene therapy was not available, Seersha would have had to match with an unrelated donor or a parent,” Dr. Kohn says. “These treatments are much more complicated. They need more chemotherapy. They need immune suppression. So that would have been a longer, harder road.”

Moving forward
Although chemotherapy, medications, infusions and injections were not easy to endure, Seersha remained in high spirits.

“After treatment, we took Seersha home, and for her, it was just another normal day,” says her mother. “She was just ready. Every time we would go to visit the doctor, she would always ask, ‘Can I do more yet?’”

The answer soon became yes.

Seersha is now healthy, with her immune system responding well to the gene therapy treatment. She enjoys exploring the outdoors, playing at the park, learning through homeschool, trying new sports such as softball, and making friends.

“She’s a huge advocate for herself. She’s not shy. She just takes it all in stride,” Shayla Sulack says. “And the fact that she gets to enjoy whatever everybody else does, you know, going to the beach, or even going to the grocery store. It's just simple ups from here.”

“She has grown — you just see the maturation,” Dr. Kohn adds. “She was a baby when we treated her, and now, she’s become a young girl. It is a wonderful blessing to be able to improve people’s lives.”

At the same time, Seersha’s journey has become an inspiration to many. She and her family are dedicated to sharing her story, advocating for other children with ADA-SCID, and offering support to families navigating similar paths.

There's just this huge community of SCID parents, and so, that's all we do, we try to advocate for them to get them the treatments that they need,” says Shayla Sulack.

Reflecting on Seersha’s journey, her mother shares heartfelt advice for families: “Don’t do it alone.”

“It is a terrifying moment when your child is sick,” she says. “You want to close the entire world out to protect your child, but accept the help that is there — because there is help and community.”

Dr. Kohn agrees. “It is a very difficult road, but there’s light at the end, as you can see with Seersha.

“UCLA Health has been a leader in gene therapy for childhood diseases like this,” he says. “The resources that we have — including the transplant program and the laboratories that can process these cells — are unique. We are really one of the few places in the country that offer these kinds of treatments.”

As Seersha’s family — which recently welcomed a new baby — prepares to move to Tennessee, their gratitude for UCLA Health continues to grow.

“We don't want to leave UCLA — we want UCLA to travel with us,” Shayla Sulack says with a smile. “Seersha has been with the UCLA Health team for almost eight years, and they've been with our family since then. They just feel like family.”

Dem Who Screamed for Hegseth Impeachment Misses Vote, Blames Being “Trapped” by Police Motorcade

House Democrat Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico was one of 11 members of her party who failed to show up for the high-profile vote to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth. When Fox News reporter Bill Melugin caught her outside the Capitol, she offered a traffic jam as the reason.

“As I mentioned just now, I was trapped right there at that street corner because there was a police motorcade moving buses off of the campus and I physically was trapped right at that corner in my vehicle in traffic because the police had shut down traffic in both directions,” Stansbury said.

Melugin pressed her on the timing. The vote had been public since Monday night. Once Republicans set it for around 5:30 p.m., the House left it open longer than the planned 15 minutes. “So why not come here sooner though?” he asked.

Stansbury repeated the claim. “Because I did, and I was trapped in my vehicle because of the police motorcade.”

When Melugin noted that traffic might not land as a convincing excuse for a vote her party had treated as a priority, she pushed back. “It was not open for a while. They gaveled the vote as soon as they could.”

Several House Democrats have already voiced frustration with colleagues who missed the roll call after months of demanding Hegseth’s impeachment. Nancy Pelosi’s office confirmed she was not even in Washington; she was in San Francisco when the vote occurred.

Melugin later told the studio the explanation looked thin. The Hill had known the vote was coming since Monday, the window stayed open past the initial 15 minutes, and Democrats had spent weeks calling the issue a top priority. “If they had all been here, there’s a chance that Hegseth may have been impeached in the House,” he said. Instead, the effort failed, and Democrats will have to wait until they potentially regain the majority in January to try again.

The episode left the on-camera exchange as the clearest public accounting of why one of the loudest voices for impeachment was absent when the votes were counted.
